text:
Its most useful summary is the expected value, the long-run average. Take a loaded die that lands on six half the time, and on each other face a tenth. Multiply each face by its chance, and add. Four point five. Picture the chances as weights on a beam. It balances at four and a half... which isn't a face on the die, and isn't the likeliest roll, either. That's six. Roll it half a million times in code, and the average comes out four point five. Its spread is the variance, the average squared distance from that mean. Three point two five. Its square root, the standard deviation, is about one point eight. And that long-run average is how you weigh a decision.

A store sells an eighty-dollar warranty. It pays out three hundred if the device fails, and fifteen percent of them do. So the expected payout is fifteen percent of three hundred, forty-five dollars. The store expects to keep thirty-five per warranty. Sell a million in code, and the average profit is thirty-five dollars and five cents. Good for the store... and, on average, a losing bet for the buyer. But an average is for a gamble you face many times. For one loss you couldn't survive, the spread matters MORE... which is why people buy insurance at all. An expected value and a variance sum up one random variable. And many random variables share a handful of familiar shapes... the named distributions.
